question: What is the structural difference between an Array and a Singly Linked List in memory layout and element access?
ideal_answer: An Array allocates contiguous memory locations, allowing O(1) random element access via index arithmetic and maximizing CPU cache locality. A Singly Linked List allocates non-contiguous nodes containing data and pointers to the next node. Accessing an element in a Linked List requires O(n) sequential traversal from the head node.
key_points: Arrays use contiguous memory allocation enabling O(1) index access and optimal CPU caching
Linked Lists use non-contiguous node allocations with next-pointers, requiring O(n) sequential access
Inserting at the head of a linked list is O(1), whereas inserting in an array requires O(n) element shifting
red_flags: Claiming linked lists allow O(1) random access by index
Assuming arrays can dynamically expand without memory reallocation
follow_ups: How does a Doubly Linked List differ from a Singly Linked List in pointer memory and deletion overhead?
Why do dynamic array implementations double capacity when full?

question: How does a Hash Table achieve average-case O(1) time complexity for lookup operations?
ideal_answer: A Hash Table maps keys to bucket array indices using a hash function that computes a numerical hash code modulo the array size. When retrieving a key, the hash function locates the target array bucket in O(1) time. In cases of hash collisions (multiple keys hashing to the same bucket), collision resolution techniques like chaining or open addressing resolve candidate matches.
key_points: Hash functions transform keys into numerical array bucket indices in O(1) time
Average-case lookup, insertion, and deletion operate in O(1) time complexity
Collisions are resolved via separate chaining (linked lists/trees) or open addressing (linear probing)
red_flags: Claiming Hash Tables guarantee worst-case O(1) time complexity under heavy collisions
Confusing hash table buckets with binary search tree pointers
follow_ups: What happens to Hash Table performance when all keys degrade to the same hash bucket?
How does Java 8 HashMap optimize heavy collisions by replacing linked lists with Red-Black trees?

question: How does a Binary Search Tree (BST) operate, and when does its lookup performance degrade to O(n)?
ideal_answer: A Binary Search Tree maintains the invariant that for any node, all left subtree values are smaller and all right subtree values are larger. In a balanced BST, search, insertion, and deletion take O(log n) time by halving search space at each step. If elements are inserted in strictly sorted order without rebalancing, the tree degrades into a skewed linked list, causing operations to degrade to O(n) worst-case.
key_points: BST property: left subtree < root < right subtree for all nodes
Balanced BST yields O(log n) search, insertion, and deletion time complexity
Unbalanced/skewed BSTs degrade to O(n) linear search complexity when inputs are sorted
red_flags: Claiming standard BSTs automatically self-balance on every insertion
Confusing in-order traversal with level-order breadth-first search
follow_ups: How do self-balancing trees like AVL or Red-Black Trees prevent BST skewing?
What tree traversal order prints a Binary Search Tree's elements in sorted order?

question: How does a Min-Heap structure support efficient Priority Queue operations?
ideal_answer: A Min-Heap is a complete binary tree backed by an array where every parent node holds a value smaller than or equal to its children. Finding the minimum element takes O(1) time by inspecting the root index [0]. Inserting an element or removing the root minimum takes O(log n) time by percolating up or sifting down elements along tree height to restore heap order.
key_points: Min-Heap property: parent node value <= child node values throughout complete binary tree
Root element at index [0] provides O(1) minimum element access
Insert and extract-min operate in O(log n) time via heapify/sift operations
red_flags: Claiming searching for an arbitrary non-root element in a Min-Heap takes O(1) time
Confusing Min-Heap ordering with Binary Search Tree ordering
follow_ups: How do array index formulas (2i + 1, 2i + 2) locate child nodes in an array-backed heap?
What is the time complexity of building a heap (Heapify) from an unsorted array of size n?

question: How do QuickSort and MergeSort compare in time complexity, space overhead, and algorithm stability?
ideal_answer: QuickSort uses divide-and-conquer partitioning around a pivot, achieving average O(n log n) time and O(log n) in-place stack space, but degrades to O(n^2) time on bad pivot selection; it is unstable. MergeSort guarantees deterministic O(n log n) time across all cases and is stable, preserving equal element ordering. However, MergeSort requires O(n) auxiliary space to store sub-arrays during merge steps.
key_points: QuickSort: average O(n log n), worst-case O(n^2), in-place O(log n) space, unstable
MergeSort: guaranteed O(n log n) time across all cases, O(n) auxiliary space, stable
Stability preserves relative order of duplicate elements; QuickSort is preferred in-memory
red_flags: Claiming MergeSort operates in O(1) auxiliary space without extra sub-arrays
Believing QuickSort worst-case time complexity is O(n log n)
follow_ups: How does randomized pivot selection or Median-of-Three prevent QuickSort O(n^2) degradation?
What is Timsort, and how does it combine MergeSort and InsertionSort for real-world languages?

question: How do self-balancing Red-Black Trees maintain logarithmic height bounds during insertions?
ideal_answer: Red-Black Trees are self-balancing binary search trees where each node holds a color attribute (Red or Black) and obeys strict balancing rules: the root is Black, no two adjacent nodes can be Red (no Red-Red parent-child), and every path from a node to descendant null leaves contains identical Black node counts. Insertions color new nodes Red and restore properties using tree rotations and color flips in O(log n) time.
key_points: Enforces strict node coloring constraints guaranteeing longest path <= 2 * shortest path
No consecutive Red nodes and equal Black-height across all paths to null leaves
Restores balance after insertion using local tree rotations (left/right) and recoloring in O(log n) time
red_flags: Claiming Red-Black trees require full tree rebuilds on every insertion
Confusing Red-Black tree strict height bounds with AVL tree height balance factors
follow_ups: How do AVL trees differ from Red-Black trees in balance strictness and lookup speed?
Why are Red-Black trees preferred for implementing C++ std::map and Java TreeMap?

question: What is Big-O notation, and why does it focus on upper-bound asymptotic growth rather than exact execution runtime?
ideal_answer: Big-O notation describes the upper bound of an algorithm's growth rate in time or memory as input size n approaches infinity. It ignores hardware-dependent CPU speeds, compiler optimizations, and constant factors to provide a standardized, machine-independent metric. Focusing on worst-case asymptotic bounds guarantees performance behavior under scale.
key_points: Big-O characterizes asymptotic upper bound growth rate of time/space as n approaches infinity
Drops low-order terms and constant multipliers (e.g. 3n^2 + 5n -> O(n^2))
Provides machine-independent performance evaluation focused on scaling behavior
red_flags: Including constant multipliers inside Big-O expressions (e.g. writing O(2N) instead of O(N))
Confusing Big-O (upper bound) with Big-Omega (lower bound) or Big-Theta (tight bound)
follow_ups: What is the mathematical definition of Big-O involving constants c and n_0?
Why do algorithms with higher constant factors sometimes run faster for small inputs n?

question: What is the time complexity of Binary Search on a sorted array of size n, and why?
ideal_answer: Binary Search has a time complexity of O(log n). It operates by comparing the target value against the array's midpoint element. If they do not match, it eliminates half of the remaining search space in a single comparison step. Reducing the search space by half at each step requires log2(n) comparisons to locate the target or conclude it is absent.
key_points: Binary search runs in O(log n) logarithmic time complexity
Halves remaining candidate search space in a single comparison step
Requires array to be pre-sorted before binary search can be applied
red_flags: Claiming binary search works on unsorted contiguous arrays
Confusing logarithmic time O(log n) with linear time O(n)
follow_ups: Why does binary search require random access array storage rather than singly linked lists?
How do you prevent integer overflow when calculating midpoint mid = low + (high - low) / 2?

question: Why is array access by index O(1) time complexity, whereas searching for an unindexed value is O(n)?
ideal_answer: Arrays store elements in contiguous memory. Accessing an index computes target memory address in O(1) constant time using base math: Address = Base_Address + Index * Element_Size. Searching for an unindexed value requires linearly scanning array elements one by one from start to end, resulting in O(n) worst-case time complexity.
key_points: Contiguous memory enables direct address calculation in O(1) time: Base + Index * Size
Searching for a specific value requires linear iteration through array elements in O(n) time
Index access cost is independent of total array size n
red_flags: Claiming array index lookup requires traversing array elements sequentially
Confusing element value search with index access
follow_ups: How does CPU L1/L2 cache prefetching benefit contiguous array traversal?
What is the time complexity of inserting an element at the middle of an array?

question: What is the difference between Auxiliary Space Complexity and Total Space Complexity?
ideal_answer: Auxiliary Space Complexity measures only the extra or temporary memory allocated by an algorithm during execution (like call stacks or scratch arrays), excluding input data size. Total Space Complexity includes both the memory occupied by input data plus auxiliary memory allocated by the algorithm. Algorithms are evaluated on auxiliary space to measure pure overhead.
key_points: Auxiliary space counts temporary memory allocated by algorithm execution excluding input data
Total space counts input data storage plus auxiliary temporary space
In-place algorithms require O(1) auxiliary space regardless of input size
red_flags: Including input data size when calculating auxiliary space for in-place algorithms
Ignoring recursive call stack memory overhead when computing space complexity
follow_ups: What is the auxiliary space complexity of iterative versus recursive depth-first search (DFS)?
Why does Tail Call Optimization (TCO) reduce recursive auxiliary space to O(1)?

question: What is Amortized Time Complexity, and how does it apply to dynamic array append operations?
ideal_answer: Amortized time complexity averages the execution cost of a sequence of operations over time, ensuring that rare expensive operations are spread across many cheap operations. Appending to a dynamic array takes O(1) time when capacity remains. When capacity is reached, the array allocates double its size and copies n elements in an O(n) operation. Averaged over n appends, total cost is O(n), giving an amortized O(1) time per append.
key_points: Amortized analysis calculates average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence
Dynamic array append is O(1) most of the time; resizing allocates new 2x memory and copies n items in O(n)
Spreading the infrequent O(n) resize across n appends yields O(1) amortized cost per append
red_flags: Claiming every single dynamic array append takes strictly O(1) worst-case time
Confusing amortized time complexity with average-case probabilistic complexity
follow_ups: What happens to amortized append cost if dynamic array growth factor is 1.5x vs 2x?
What is the Accounting Method or Banker's Method in amortized analysis?

question: How do you apply the Master Theorem to determine the asymptotic time complexity of divide-and-conquer recurrence relations?
ideal_answer: The Master Theorem solves divide-and-conquer recurrences of the form T(n) = a * T(n/b) + f(n), where a >= 1 and b > 1. It compares f(n) against n^(log_b a), representing work at non-leaf nodes versus leaves. If n^(log_b a) dominates polynomially, T(n) = Theta(n^(log_b a)). If f(n) and n^(log_b a) are asymptotically equal, T(n) = Theta(n^(log_b a) * log n). If f(n) dominates, T(n) = Theta(f(n)).
key_points: Solves recurrences T(n) = a * T(n/b) + f(n) for divide-and-conquer algorithms
Compares divide work f(n) with leaf node work n^(log_b a)
3 cases: leaf-dominated Theta(n^(log_b a)), balanced Theta(n^(log_b a) log n), or root-dominated Theta(f(n))
red_flags: Applying Master Theorem to non-polynomially bounded divide work or non-constant subproblems
Misidentifying parameters a (number of subproblems) and b (subproblem division factor)
follow_ups: What is the Master Theorem case for MergeSort where T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)?
Why can't the standard Master Theorem solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n directly without extensions?

question: What is Encapsulation in Object-Oriented Programming, and how does it protect object state?
ideal_answer: Encapsulation bundles data variables and the methods that operate on them within a single class unit, while restricting direct external access to internal state using access modifiers (private/protected). External callers modify state exclusively through public methods (getters/setters/methods) that enforce validation logic. This hides internal representation details and prevents arbitrary state corruption.
key_points: Bundles data fields and related operating methods inside a single class object
Restricts direct field access using private/protected access modifiers
Exposes controlled public methods that validate and maintain object invariants
red_flags: Making all internal class fields public without restriction
Confusing encapsulation with class inheritance
follow_ups: How do getters and setters enforce data validation and business invariants?
What is the difference between private, protected, and public access modifiers?

question: What is Polymorphism in Object-Oriented Programming, and how do compile-time and runtime polymorphism differ?
ideal_answer: Polymorphism enables objects of different derived classes to be treated as instances of a shared base interface. Compile-time polymorphism (method overloading) resolves method signatures during compilation based on parameter types and counts. Runtime polymorphism (method overriding) resolves concrete method calls at execution time via dynamic dispatch using virtual method tables (vtables).
key_points: Allows uniform interface invocations across varying underlying class implementations
Compile-time polymorphism (overloading) resolves method calls based on argument signature at compile time
Runtime polymorphism (overriding) resolves concrete derived class methods at runtime via virtual dispatch
red_flags: Claiming method overloading occurs at runtime via virtual tables
Confusing method overriding in subclasses with method overloading in the same class
follow_ups: How does a virtual method table (vtable) work under the hood in C++ or Java?
What is an abstract class versus an interface in object-oriented design?

question: How does Abstraction differ from Encapsulation in Object-Oriented System Design?
ideal_answer: Abstraction focuses on hiding complex implementation details behind clean, high-level interface contracts, exposing only 'what' an object does rather than 'how' it works. Encapsulation focuses on bundling state and restricting access to internal fields to protect 'how' data is stored and modified. Interfaces and abstract classes achieve abstraction; private fields and public methods achieve encapsulation.
key_points: Abstraction hides internal implementation complexity behind high-level interfaces ('what')
Encapsulation restricts direct access to internal state fields ('how')
Abstraction simplifies design usability; encapsulation guarantees data integrity and safety
red_flags: Treating Abstraction and Encapsulation as identical concepts
Claiming abstraction requires making all class members private
follow_ups: How do interface contracts promote modularity and testability?
Why should client code depend on abstract interfaces rather than concrete implementations?

question: What is the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) in SOLID design, and what problems occur when it is violated?
ideal_answer: The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) dictates that a class or module should have one, and only one, reason to change. It means a class should focus on a single cohesive responsibility or actor goal. Violating SRP produces 'God classes' that combine unrelated business logic (e.g. database persistence, UI formatting, authentication), making code fragile, difficult to unit test, and prone to regression bugs.
key_points: A class should have only one reason to change, focusing on a single cohesive responsibility
Prevents tightly-coupled 'God classes' that mix distinct business concerns
Improves maintainability, code readability, and unit test isolation
red_flags: Interpreting SRP as 'a class should only contain a single method'
Mixing database querying, business logic, and HTTP response formatting in one service class
follow_ups: How do you refactor a monolith controller class that violates SRP into clean service modules?
How does SRP interact with the Open/Closed Principle (OCP)?

question: What is the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP), and how does Dependency Injection (DI) fulfill it?
ideal_answer: The Dependency Inversion Principle states that high-level business modules should not depend directly on low-level concrete implementation modules; both should depend on abstract interfaces. Dependency Injection (DI) fulfills DIP by passing (injecting) concrete dependencies into a class via constructor parameters or frameworks rather than instantiating dependencies internally using new. This decoupling enables easy mock injection for unit testing.
key_points: High-level modules and low-level modules depend on shared abstract interface contracts
Classes receive dependencies from external callers rather than instantiating concrete classes internally
Dramatically improves code testability by enabling mock/stub injection in unit tests
red_flags: Instantiating concrete database or API client dependencies directly inside business constructors
Confusing Dependency Inversion Principle (architectural rule) with Dependency Injection (implementation pattern)
follow_ups: What is an Inversion of Control (IoC) container in frameworks like Spring or NestJS?
What is constructor injection versus setter injection?

question: How does the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) guide inheritance, and what classic example demonstrates its violation?
ideal_answer: The Liskov Substitution Principle states that objects of a derived class must be seamlessly substitutable for objects of their base class without breaking program correctness or altering expected behavioral invariants. A classic violation occurs when Square inherits from Rectangle. Setting width and height independently works for Rectangle, but forced equal-side logic in Square breaks callers expecting independent dimensions.
key_points: Subclasses must fulfill all behavioral contracts and invariants of base classes without error
Callers operating on base references must work correctly when passed any derived instance
Classic violation: Square inheriting from Rectangle breaks expected independent width/height behavior
red_flags: Overriding base methods to throw NotImplementedException or do nothing
Assuming LSP is satisfied merely by passing compile-time method signature checks
follow_ups: Why is 'Composition over Inheritance' often recommended to prevent LSP violations?
How do pre-conditions and post-conditions behave under LSP in derived classes?

question: What is the key difference between a Process and a Thread in operating systems?
ideal_answer: A Process is an isolated execution instance with its own virtual address space, file descriptor table, page tables, and memory security context. A Thread is an execution unit within a process that shares virtual memory, global data, and file descriptors with sibling threads, maintaining only its own execution stack, registers, and program counter. Threads enable low-overhead concurrency within shared memory.
key_points: Process maintains isolated virtual memory space, page tables, and file descriptors
Thread executes inside a process, sharing heap, global memory, and file descriptors with sibling threads
Inter-process communication (IPC) requires OS overhead; inter-thread communication shares process heap
red_flags: Claiming threads in different processes share the same virtual address space
Believing processes do not incur memory isolation overhead
follow_ups: What Inter-Process Communication (IPC) mechanisms enable processes to exchange data?
Why does a process crash terminate all its threads, while a thread crash can corrupt process heap?

question: What is Virtual Memory, and how do Page Tables enable physical memory isolation?
ideal_answer: Virtual Memory is an OS abstraction that provides each process with the illusion of a vast, contiguous address space. The CPU Memory Management Unit (MMU) translates virtual addresses to physical RAM addresses using Page Tables. Page Tables enforce hardware-level memory protection, preventing processes from reading or writing into another process's physical memory space.
key_points: Provides processes with independent, contiguous virtual address space abstractions
MMU translates virtual pages to physical RAM frames via Page Tables
Enforces memory isolation and security, preventing processes from corrupting each other's memory
red_flags: Claiming virtual memory addresses correspond 1-to-1 directly to physical RAM chips without translation
Confusing virtual memory paging with disk swap memory
follow_ups: What is a Page Fault, and how does the OS kernel handle it?
What is the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB), and how does it speed up address translation?

question: What occurs during a Context Switch, and why is switching between processes more expensive than switching between threads?
ideal_answer: A Context Switch saves the current CPU execution state (registers, stack pointer, program counter) and restores the state of the next scheduled thread or process. Switching between processes is significantly more expensive because it requires flushing the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB), updating CPU page table base registers (CR3), and invalidating CPU cache lines due to virtual address space changes.
key_points: Saves current CPU registers, stack pointer, and program counter; restores next thread/process state
Process context switch requires changing page tables (CR3 register) and flushing TLB caches
Thread context switch within the same process retains memory mappings, avoiding TLB flush overhead
red_flags: Claiming thread context switching within a process flushes page tables and TLB
Believing context switches execute with zero CPU clock cycle overhead
follow_ups: What is CPU cache line invalidation and cold cache penalty after a context switch?
How do user-space cooperative fibers/coroutines avoid OS kernel context switches?

question: What are the four Coffman conditions required for Deadlock to occur in an operating system?
ideal_answer: Deadlock occurs when a set of concurrent processes are permanently blocked, each holding a resource while waiting for another held resource. The four necessary Coffman conditions are: 1) Mutual Exclusion (non-shareable resources), 2) Hold and Wait (processes hold resources while requesting new ones), 3) No Preemption (resources cannot be forcibly taken), and 4) Circular Wait (a closed chain of processes waiting on each other).
key_points: Mutual Exclusion: at least one resource is held in a non-shareable mode
Hold and Wait: process holding resources requests additional resources held by others
No Preemption & Circular Wait: resources cannot be forcibly confiscated, creating a circular dependency chain
red_flags: Believing breaking just 1 of the 4 conditions is insufficient to prevent deadlock
Confusing deadlock (permanent block) with starvation (indefinite delay)
follow_ups: How does global resource lock ordering eliminate the Circular Wait condition?
What is Banker's Algorithm for deadlock avoidance?

question: How does a Mutex lock differ from a Counting Semaphore in thread synchronization?
ideal_answer: A Mutex (Mutual Exclusion) is a locking mechanism ownership constraint where only the specific thread that locked the mutex can unlock it, allowing a single thread into a critical section. A Counting Semaphore is a signaling mechanism maintaining an integer counter; any thread can signal (increment) or wait on (decrement) the semaphore, regulating access to a resource pool of N capacity.
key_points: Mutex enforces single-thread ownership: only the thread that acquired the lock can release it
Counting Semaphore regulates concurrent access to a fixed capacity pool of N resources
Semaphores act as signaling mechanisms; Mutexes act as locking mechanisms
red_flags: Allowing any random thread to unlock a Mutex held by another thread
Treating a binary semaphore as completely identical to a Mutex with ownership rules
follow_ups: What is Priority Inversion, and how does Priority Inheritance resolve it in Mutexes?
What is a Spinlock, and when is it preferred over a blocking kernel Mutex?

question: What is False Sharing in multi-threaded programming, and how do software engineers prevent it?
ideal_answer: False Sharing occurs when threads running on independent CPU cores modify independent variables that reside on the same L1/L2 CPU cache line (typically 64 bytes). Whenever one core writes to its variable, the MESI cache coherency protocol invalidates the entire cache line in other cores, forcing expensive main memory syncs despite no true data dependency. Engineers prevent it using cache line padding (@Contended) to space variables across distinct cache lines.
key_points: Occurs when independent variables assigned to different CPU cores reside on the same 64-byte cache line
MESI cache coherency protocol forces frequent cache line invalidations and bus re-syncs
Prevented by padding data structures (@Contended) so core variables occupy isolated cache lines
red_flags: Confusing False Sharing with true data race conditions on shared variables
Believing CPU cache coherency is managed manually in application source code
follow_ups: How does the MESI (Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid) protocol maintain CPU cache consistency?
How does L1/L2 cache locality impact lock-free data structures like Disruptor ring buffers?

question: What are the ACID properties in Relational Database Management Systems?
ideal_answer: ACID guarantees database transaction reliability. Atomicity ensures all operations in a transaction complete successfully or all roll back completely. Consistency guarantees the database transitions from one valid schema state to another. Isolation ensures concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other. Durability guarantees committed transaction changes persist permanently, even through system crashes.
key_points: Atomicity: All-or-nothing execution of transaction statements
Consistency: Enforces database constraints, foreign keys, and schema rules before and after transactions
Isolation & Durability: Prevents concurrent transaction interference; guarantees committed writes survive power failure
red_flags: Claiming Atomicity means transactions execute fast in a single clock cycle
Confusing Isolation levels with Durability crash-recovery guarantees
follow_ups: How does a Write-Ahead Log (WAL) ensure Durability during unexpected power outages?
What is two-phase commit (2PC) in distributed transactions?

question: What is Database Normalization, and what anomaly does First Normal Form (1NF) resolve?
ideal_answer: Database Normalization organizes relational schema tables to eliminate data redundancy and prevent insertion, update, and deletion anomalies. First Normal Form (1NF) requires that every table column contains atomic (indivisible) single values, eliminating repeating groups or arrays stored inside a single column cell. It also requires a primary key to uniquely identify each row.
key_points: Normalization structures tables to eliminate redundancy and data modification anomalies
1NF enforces atomic, indivisible values per cell and removes multi-value arrays/lists
1NF requires each table row to be uniquely identifiable via a Primary Key
red_flags: Storing comma-separated text strings inside a single database column cell in 1NF
Assuming normalization increases read query execution speed by adding duplicate columns
follow_ups: What is the difference between Second Normal Form (2NF) and Third Normal Form (3NF)?
When is Denormalization intentionally applied in analytical data warehouses (OLAP)?

question: How do Primary Keys, Foreign Keys, and Unique Indexes differ in relational database design?
ideal_answer: A Primary Key uniquely identifies each record in a table, enforces NOT NULL constraints, and creates the clustered index in engines like InnoDB. A Foreign Key enforces referential integrity between tables by linking a column to a primary key in another table, preventing orphan records. A Unique Index enforces uniqueness for non-primary columns, allowing at most one NULL value in standard SQL.
key_points: Primary Key: uniquely identifies rows, cannot contain NULLs, sets default clustered index layout
Foreign Key: maintains referential integrity between parent and child tables
Unique Index: enforces unique values across non-primary columns, allowing NULL handling based on SQL engine
red_flags: Allowing NULL values in a Primary Key column
Claiming a table can possess multiple Primary Keys
follow_ups: What is a Composite Primary Key?
What happens during DELETE operations when a Foreign Key specifies ON DELETE CASCADE?

question: Why do relational database engines use B+ Trees rather than standard Binary Search Trees for disk-based indexing?
ideal_answer: B+ Trees are multi-way self-balancing search trees optimized for disk storage. Unlike binary trees, B+ Tree nodes have high fan-out (hundreds of keys per node), matching disk block sizes and minimizing disk I/O read operations. Furthermore, all actual record data pointers are kept in leaf nodes, which are doubly-linked together, allowing O(log N) point lookups and extremely fast sequential range scans.
key_points: High fan-out matches disk page block sizes, drastically reducing disk I/O head seeks
All data records reside in leaf nodes; internal nodes store only search routing keys
Doubly-linked leaf node chains enable high-speed sequential range queries
red_flags: Claiming standard binary search trees match disk block hardware efficiency
Assuming B+ Trees store table row data inside internal routing nodes
follow_ups: What is a Clustered Index versus a Non-Clustered (Secondary) Index?
Why is index fragmentation created when random UUIDs are used as B+ Tree primary keys?

question: What are Transaction Isolation Levels, and what is a Dirty Read?
ideal_answer: Transaction Isolation Levels (Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable) control how concurrent database transactions observe intermediate uncommitted data. A Dirty Read occurs at the 'Read Uncommitted' level when Transaction A reads data modified by Transaction B before Transaction B commits. If Transaction B subsequently rolls back, Transaction A operated on invalid data that never existed.
key_points: Isolation levels trade off transaction concurrency against read anomaly vulnerabilities
Dirty Read: Reading uncommitted data written by a concurrent transaction that later rolls back
Read Committed prevents Dirty Reads; Repeatable Read prevents Non-Repeatable Reads; Serializable prevents Phantoms
red_flags: Claiming Read Committed level prevents Phantom Reads
Believing highest isolation (Serializable) carries zero performance or lock contention cost
follow_ups: What is a Non-Repeatable Read versus a Phantom Read?
How does Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) enable non-blocking reads in PostgreSQL?

question: How do Optimistic Concurrency Control and Pessimistic Concurrency Control manage concurrent updates?
ideal_answer: Pessimistic Concurrency Control assumes conflict will occur and locks target database rows immediately (e.g. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), blocking other transactions until commit; it prevents conflicts but lowers throughput. Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) assumes conflicts are rare, allowing transactions to read and modify data without locks. Before commit, OCC checks a version or timestamp column; if modified concurrently, the transaction aborts and retries.
key_points: Pessimistic Locking uses explicit row locks (FOR UPDATE), blocking concurrent writes; best for high contention
Optimistic Locking checks a version column during UPDATE without blocking reads; best for low contention
OCC yields higher system throughput under low conflict; Pessimistic prevents frequent retry aborts under high conflict
red_flags: Believing Optimistic Locking acquires exclusive database row locks during read phases
Using Pessimistic row locking for long-lived disconnected web form edits across user sessions
follow_ups: How do you construct an Optimistic Locking SQL UPDATE statement using version numbers?
What is Deadlock detection in Pessimistic locking database systems?

question: What are the primary operational differences between TCP and UDP transport protocols?
ideal_answer: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is a connection-oriented, reliable protocol that guarantees ordered packet delivery, error checking, flow control, and congestion management via a connection handshake. UDP (User Datagram Protocol) is a connectionless, lightweight protocol that sends datagrams without establishing a connection, offering no delivery guarantees or ordering but providing minimal latency.
key_points: TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, ordered delivery, flow/congestion control (web, SSH, APIs)
UDP: connectionless, unreliable, unordered, zero handshake latency (DNS, streaming, gaming)
TCP uses packet acknowledgments and retransmissions; UDP discards lost packets without retry
red_flags: Claiming UDP guarantees ordered packet delivery without application-layer code
Using TCP for real-time multiplayer game position streaming where low latency beats retransmissions
follow_ups: What fields in the TCP header enable sequence tracking and packet reordering?
Why is DNS query traffic traditionally transmitted over UDP on port 53?

question: What sequence of packets occurs during the TCP Three-Way Handshake?
ideal_answer: The TCP Three-Way Handshake establishes a reliable connection between client and server. 1) Client sends a SYN packet with a random initial sequence number (ISN_C). 2) Server responds with SYN-ACK, acknowledging ISN_C + 1 and sending its own sequence number (ISN_S). 3) Client returns an ACK packet acknowledging ISN_S + 1. The connection transitions to ESTABLISHED.
key_points: Step 1: Client -> SYN (sets initial client sequence number)
Step 2: Server -> SYN-ACK (acknowledges client SYN and sends server sequence number)
Step 3: Client -> ACK (acknowledges server SYN, connection established)
red_flags: Reversing SYN and ACK packet order during the handshake sequence
Believing data payload transmission occurs before the 3-way handshake completes

question: What is the Domain Name System (DNS), and how does recursive DNS resolution operate?
ideal_answer: DNS is a distributed hierarchical lookup system that translates human-readable domain names (api.example.com) into numerical IP addresses. In recursive resolution, a client queries a Recursive Resolver. If not cached, the resolver queries the Root DNS server for .com TLD servers, then queries the TLD server for example.com's Authoritative Name Server, and finally queries the Authoritative server to get the A/AAAA IP record.
key_points: Translates human-readable domain names into IP routing addresses
Hierarchical resolution: Recursive Resolver -> Root Server -> TLD Server -> Authoritative Server
Caches IP records according to Time-To-Live (TTL) values to accelerate future lookups
red_flags: Claiming Authoritative DNS servers resolve all world domain queries from a single centralized database
Ignoring TTL caching mechanisms in DNS resolvers
follow_ups: What is the difference between A, AAAA, CNAME, and MX DNS record types?
How does DNS Round Robin achieve basic geographical load balancing?

question: How does HTTP/2 improve performance over HTTP/1.1 for modern web applications?
ideal_answer: HTTP/1.1 suffers from Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking because requests over a single TCP connection must be processed sequentially, forcing browsers to open multiple parallel connections. HTTP/2 introduces binary framing and multiplexing, allowing multiple concurrent request/response streams over a single TCP connection. HTTP/2 also adds HPACK header compression and Server Push capabilities.
key_points: Replaces plain text with a binary framing layer for request/response handling
Multiplexing allows multiple concurrent requests over a single TCP connection, ending HTTP HoL blocking
Adds HPACK header compression to reduce HTTP metadata bandwidth consumption
red_flags: Believing HTTP/2 operates over UDP instead of TCP
Confusing HTTP Head-of-Line blocking with TCP packet loss blocking
follow_ups: How does HTTP/3 solve TCP Head-of-Line blocking by utilizing QUIC over UDP?
Why is domain sharding obsolete under HTTP/2 multiplexing?

question: How does TLS 1.3 achieve secure cryptographic session establishment with a single Round-Trip Time (1-RTT)?
ideal_answer: TLS 1.2 required 2-RTT handshakes to negotiate cipher suites and exchange keys before sending encrypted data. TLS 1.3 reduces this to 1-RTT by embedding Diffie-Hellman key exchange parameters directly inside the initial ClientHello message. The server responds with ServerHello and its certificate, allowing both sides to derive symmetric session keys immediately. TLS 1.3 also supports 0-RTT session resumption for returning clients.
key_points: Reduces handshake latency from 2-RTT (TLS 1.2) to 1-RTT by guessing key exchange parameters in ClientHello
Uses Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (ECDHE) for Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS)
Removes insecure legacy cipher algorithms (MD5, SHA1, RC4, RSA key exchange)
red_flags: Claiming TLS 1.3 uses symmetric encryption to exchange asymmetric public keys
Assuming 0-RTT session resumption is immune to replay attacks without anti-replay defenses
follow_ups: What is Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS) in TLS handshakes?
How does Server Name Indication (SNI) allow a single IP address to host multiple TLS certificates?

question: What is the core difference between Vertical Scaling (Scaling Up) and Horizontal Scaling (Scaling Out)?
ideal_answer: Vertical Scaling increases the hardware capacity of an existing single server by adding more CPU cores, RAM, or faster storage. It requires zero application code changes but hits strict hardware ceilings and creates a single point of failure. Horizontal Scaling adds more independent server instances to a pool behind a load balancer, providing virtually unlimited elasticity and fault tolerance.
key_points: Vertical Scaling: Adds hardware capacity (CPU/RAM) to a single machine; simple but bounded by physical limits
Horizontal Scaling: Adds more server nodes to a distributed pool; highly scalable and fault tolerant
Horizontal scaling requires stateless application design and distributed state management
red_flags: Claiming vertical scaling eliminates single points of failure without standby replicas
Assuming horizontal scaling requires zero network or application architecture changes
follow_ups: Why are relational databases harder to scale horizontally than stateless web servers?
How does auto-scaling dynamically adjust server instance counts based on CPU metrics?

question: What is the purpose of a Load Balancer, and how does Round Robin traffic distribution work?
ideal_answer: A Load Balancer sits between incoming client traffic and backend server pools, distributing requests to prevent any single server from becoming overwhelmed. Round Robin distribution routes incoming requests sequentially across the list of available healthy servers (Server A -> Server B -> Server C -> Server A). Load balancers also perform continuous health checks to remove failing servers.
key_points: Distributes network traffic across backend server pools to maximize throughput and reliability
Round Robin algorithm routes requests sequentially down the list of active server instances
Executes health checks to automatically route traffic away from unhealthy servers
red_flags: Assuming Round Robin accounts for varying server hardware capacity or request execution time
Routing traffic to crashed servers due to missing health checks
follow_ups: How do Weighted Round Robin and Least Connections algorithms improve load balancing?
What is Layer 4 (Transport) versus Layer 7 (Application) load balancing?

question: What is Database Sharding, and how does a Shard Key determine data distribution?
ideal_answer: Database Sharding partitions a large dataset horizontally across multiple distinct database server nodes (shards). A Shard Key is a designated table column (e.g. user_id) whose value is processed by a hashing or range function to determine which specific shard stores a given record. High cardinality shard keys ensure uniform data and query distribution across nodes.
key_points: Horizontally partitions large database tables across multiple independent database server nodes
Shard Key value determines target partition node via hash or range routing functions
High cardinality shard keys prevent data hotspotting and uneven node resource utilization
red_flags: Selecting a low cardinality shard key like gender or country that causes massive data hotspots
Assuming cross-shard JOINs perform efficiently without application-level fan-out
follow_ups: What problems occur when performing cross-shard queries or cross-shard transactions?
How does consistent hashing assist when adding new database shard nodes?

question: What is the CAP Theorem in distributed system design, and why must systems choose between Consistency and Availability during network partitions?
ideal_answer: The CAP Theorem states that a distributed datastore can simultaneously guarantee at most two of three properties: Consistency (all nodes see identical data at the same time), Availability (every non-failing node returns a response), and Partition Tolerance (system operates despite network message loss). Because network partitions (P) are inevitable in real networks, distributed systems must trade off CP (sacrificing availability to guarantee consistency) or AP (sacrificing consistency for availability).
key_points: CAP = Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance in distributed data stores
Network partitions (P) are unavoidable; systems must choose between CP or AP during network faults
CP systems reject requests or wait to ensure consistency; AP systems return stale local data to remain available
red_flags: Claiming a distributed system can guarantee CA (Consistency and Availability) while ignoring Partitions in real networks
Confusing ACID database consistency with CAP Theorem distributed read consistency
follow_ups: How does the PACELC theorem extend CAP by addressing latency trade-offs during normal operation?
What is Eventual Consistency in AP systems like Cassandra or DynamoDB?

question: How does Consistent Hashing minimize key redistribution when scaling distributed caching clusters?
ideal_answer: Standard modulo hashing hash(key) % N maps keys to N cache servers, but changing server count N forces remapping of nearly 100% of keys, causing massive cache stampedes. Consistent Hashing maps both servers and keys to positions on a virtual 360-degree hash ring using uniform hash functions. When adding or removing a server node, only k/N keys are remapped to adjacent neighbors, minimizing cache invalidation.
key_points: Standard hash(key) % N invalidates ~100% of cached keys whenever node count N changes
Consistent Hashing maps servers and keys onto a circular 2^32 hash ring space
Adding or removing a server node remaps only k/N keys to adjacent ring nodes, preventing cluster stampedes
red_flags: Claiming Consistent Hashing eliminates all key lookups entirely
Omitting virtual nodes (vnodes) which prevent hotspots and ensure uniform load distribution
follow_ups: How do virtual nodes (vnodes) prevent hotspots when physical server capacities differ?
How is Consistent Hashing applied in distributed systems like Amazon Dynamo or Cassandra?

question: What is the difference between a stack and a queue, and where is each used?
ideal_answer: A stack is LIFO: push and pop happen at one end, used for function calls, undo, and expression evaluation. A queue is FIFO: elements enter at the rear and leave from the front, used for scheduling, BFS, and buffering. Both support O(1) insert and remove when implemented with a linked list or circular array.
key_points: Stack is LIFO; queue is FIFO
Stack: call stack, undo, parsing; queue: scheduling, BFS
Both achieve O(1) core operations with proper implementation
red_flags: Mixing up LIFO and FIFO
Implementing a queue with an array and O(n) shifting on every dequeue
follow_ups: How can you implement a queue using two stacks?
What is a deque?

question: How does recursion use the call stack, and what causes a stack overflow?
ideal_answer: Each recursive call pushes a new frame with its parameters and local variables onto the call stack, and frames are popped as calls return. A correct recursion needs a base case and progress toward it. Missing base cases or very deep recursion exhaust the stack and cause a stack overflow, which can be fixed with iteration, memoization, or tail-call techniques where supported.
key_points: Each call adds a stack frame; returns pop it
Base case plus progress toward it is required
Too-deep or unbounded recursion causes stack overflow
red_flags: Writing recursion without a base case
Claiming recursion never uses extra memory
follow_ups: How would you convert a recursive DFS into an iterative one?
What is tail recursion?

question: How do BFS and DFS differ, and when do you use each?
ideal_answer: BFS explores a graph level by level using a queue and finds the shortest path in unweighted graphs. DFS goes as deep as possible using a stack or recursion and suits cycle detection, topological sort, and exploring all paths. Both run in O(V+E) time, but BFS can use more memory on wide graphs while DFS depth can be large on deep graphs.
key_points: BFS: queue, level order, shortest path in unweighted graphs
DFS: stack/recursion, cycle detection, topological sort
Both O(V+E); memory profile differs
red_flags: Using DFS to claim shortest paths in unweighted graphs
Forgetting a visited set and looping forever on cycles
follow_ups: How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph?
How would you find the shortest path in a grid with obstacles?

question: How do you detect a cycle in a linked list?
ideal_answer: Use Floyd's tortoise and hare: move a slow pointer one step and a fast pointer two steps at a time. If they ever meet, the list has a cycle; if the fast pointer reaches null, it does not. This runs in O(n) time and O(1) space, unlike the hash-set approach that needs O(n) extra space.
key_points: Slow and fast pointers meet if a cycle exists
O(n) time and O(1) space
Hash set of visited nodes also works but uses O(n) space
red_flags: Modifying node values permanently without noting it
Looping with a single pointer and no termination condition
follow_ups: How do you find the node where the cycle begins?
How would you find the middle of a linked list?

question: Explain the two-pointer and sliding window techniques with an example problem.
ideal_answer: Two pointers walk through an array from both ends or at different speeds to avoid nested loops, for example finding a pair with a target sum in a sorted array in O(n). A sliding window maintains a contiguous range and moves its edges, for example finding the longest substring without repeating characters by tracking characters in a set or map. Both usually reduce O(n^2) brute force to O(n).
key_points: Two pointers: sorted arrays, pairs, partitioning, O(n)
Sliding window: contiguous subarray or substring problems
Replaces nested loops, typically O(n^2) to O(n)
red_flags: Using the technique on unsorted data where order matters, without sorting first
Shrinking the window without updating tracked state
follow_ups: How do you find the maximum sum of a subarray of size k?
What invariant does your window maintain?

question: What is dynamic programming, and how do memoization and tabulation differ? Use an example.
ideal_answer: Dynamic programming solves problems with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure by storing results instead of recomputing them. Memoization is top-down: recursion plus a cache. Tabulation is bottom-up: fill a table iteratively from base cases. For Fibonacci, naive recursion is exponential, while either DP approach is O(n), and tabulation can cut space to O(1).
key_points: Needs overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure
Memoization is top-down with a cache; tabulation is bottom-up
Fibonacci goes from exponential to O(n)
red_flags: Calling any recursion 'dynamic programming'
Ignoring the state definition and recurrence
follow_ups: How would you solve the 0/1 knapsack problem?
How do you reduce the space of a 2D DP table?

question: How does Dijkstra's algorithm work, and why does it fail with negative edge weights?
ideal_answer: Dijkstra keeps the best known distance to each node and repeatedly picks the unvisited node with the smallest distance, using a min-heap, relaxing its outgoing edges. It relies on the assumption that once a node is finalized, no shorter path can exist, which negative edges break. With a binary heap it runs in O((V+E) log V). Use Bellman-Ford when negative weights exist.
key_points: Greedy: always finalize the closest unvisited node
Min-heap gives O((V+E) log V)
Negative edges break the finalized-node assumption; use Bellman-Ford
red_flags: Using Dijkstra on graphs with negative edges
Using BFS for weighted shortest paths
follow_ups: How does A* differ from Dijkstra?
What is the time complexity of Bellman-Ford?

question: How can a graph be represented, and when is an adjacency list better than an adjacency matrix?
ideal_answer: An adjacency matrix is a V x V grid giving O(1) edge lookup but O(V^2) space. An adjacency list stores each node's neighbors, using O(V+E) space and iterating neighbors efficiently. Lists are better for sparse graphs, while matrices suit dense graphs or frequent edge-existence checks.
key_points: Matrix: O(V^2) space, O(1) edge lookup
List: O(V+E) space, efficient neighbor traversal
List for sparse graphs, matrix for dense graphs
red_flags: Using a matrix for a huge sparse graph
Claiming the list gives O(1) edge lookup
follow_ups: How do you represent a weighted graph?
What is the cost of adding a vertex in each representation?

question: How do you reverse a singly linked list, and what is the time and space complexity?
ideal_answer: Iterate through the list while keeping prev, current, and next pointers: save next, point current.next to prev, then advance prev and current. When current is null, prev is the new head. This takes O(n) time and O(1) extra space, while the recursive version uses O(n) stack space.
key_points: Iterative pointer reversal with prev, current, next
O(n) time, O(1) extra space
Recursive version costs O(n) call-stack space
red_flags: Losing the rest of the list by overwriting next before saving it
Returning the old head instead of the new head
follow_ups: How would you reverse only a sublist between positions m and n?
How would you check whether a linked list is a palindrome?

question: How would you find the k-th largest element in an unsorted array, and what are the tradeoffs between approaches?
ideal_answer: Sorting works in O(n log n). A min-heap of size k gives O(n log k) time and O(k) space and also works on streams. Quickselect partitions around a pivot and averages O(n) time with O(1) extra space, but its worst case is O(n^2) without randomized pivots. Choose by input size, memory, and whether data arrives as a stream.
key_points: Sort: O(n log n); min-heap of size k: O(n log k)
Quickselect: average O(n), worst O(n^2)
Heap approach suits streaming data
red_flags: Using a max-heap of all n elements and ignoring the cheaper size-k heap
Claiming quickselect is always O(n)
follow_ups: How do you reduce quickselect's worst-case risk?

question: What is the difference between stack memory and heap memory?
ideal_answer: Stack memory stores function call frames and local variables, is managed automatically in LIFO order, and is very fast but small. Heap memory holds dynamically allocated objects that live until freed or garbage collected, is larger but slower, and can fragment or leak. Overusing the stack causes overflow while mismanaging the heap causes leaks.
key_points: Stack: automatic, LIFO, fast, limited size
Heap: dynamic, larger, manual or garbage-collected
Stack overflow vs memory leak as typical failures
red_flags: Saying objects always live on the stack in every language
Believing heap memory is freed automatically at function return
follow_ups: Where do primitives and objects live in Java or Python?
What is a memory leak in a garbage-collected language?

question: Compare inheritance and composition. When do you prefer composition?
ideal_answer: Inheritance models an is-a relationship and reuses behavior from a parent class, but it tightly couples subclasses to the parent and can create fragile hierarchies. Composition models has-a by holding other objects and delegating to them, giving looser coupling and runtime flexibility. The common guideline is to favor composition over inheritance unless there is a true is-a relationship.
key_points: Inheritance: is-a, tight coupling, fragile base class risk
Composition: has-a, delegation, flexible and testable
Prefer composition unless the subtype relationship is genuine
red_flags: Using inheritance only to reuse code
Claiming inheritance is always bad
follow_ups: Give an example where inheritance is the right choice.
How does composition make unit testing easier?

question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface?
ideal_answer: An abstract class can hold state, constructors, and a mix of implemented and abstract methods, and a class typically extends only one. An interface defines a contract of method signatures without state, and a class can implement many. Use an abstract class for shared base behavior in a related family, and an interface to define a capability across unrelated classes.
key_points: Abstract class: shared state and partial implementation, single inheritance
Interface: contract only, multiple implementation
Abstract class for a family, interface for a capability
red_flags: Saying a class can extend multiple abstract classes in Java
Claiming interfaces can never contain any implementation in any language
follow_ups: How do default methods change interfaces in Java?
Can an abstract class be instantiated?

question: Compare the CPU scheduling algorithms FCFS, SJF, and Round Robin.
ideal_answer: FCFS runs processes in arrival order; it is simple but short jobs can wait behind long ones (convoy effect). SJF runs the shortest job next and minimizes average waiting time, but needs burst-time knowledge and can starve long jobs. Round Robin gives each process a fixed time quantum, which suits interactive systems, with the quantum size trading responsiveness against context-switch overhead.
key_points: FCFS: simple, convoy effect
SJF: minimal average wait, starvation risk, needs burst estimates
Round Robin: time quantum, fair, context-switch overhead
red_flags: Claiming SJF can be implemented exactly without knowing burst times
Setting the Round Robin quantum to extremes without discussing tradeoffs
follow_ups: What is starvation and how does aging fix it?
What happens if the time quantum is too large or too small?

question: What happens, step by step, when you type a URL into a browser and press Enter?
ideal_answer: The browser checks caches, resolves the domain through DNS to an IP, and opens a TCP connection (plus a TLS handshake for HTTPS). It sends an HTTP request, the server processes it and returns a response, and the browser parses the HTML, fetches CSS, JS, and images, builds the DOM and render tree, and paints the page.
key_points: DNS resolution, then TCP connection and TLS handshake
HTTP request and server response
Browser parses HTML/CSS/JS, builds the DOM, and renders
red_flags: Skipping DNS or the connection setup entirely
Saying the browser downloads everything before rendering anything
follow_ups: Where can caching happen in this flow?

question: What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS?
ideal_answer: HTTP sends data in plain text, so anyone on the network path can read or alter it. HTTPS is HTTP over TLS, which encrypts the traffic, authenticates the server through a certificate, and protects integrity. It is essential for logins and payments, and it also enables features like HTTP/2 in browsers.
key_points: HTTPS = HTTP over TLS
Provides encryption, server authentication, and integrity
Required for sensitive data and modern browser features
red_flags: Saying HTTPS makes a website itself secure from all attacks
Confusing HTTPS with a different port-only change
follow_ups: What is a TLS certificate and who issues it?

question: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?
ideal_answer: Merge combines two branches by creating a merge commit and preserves the full history as it happened. Rebase replays your commits on top of another branch, producing a linear history but rewriting commit hashes. Do not rebase commits that others have already pulled; use merge for shared branches and rebase to tidy local work.
key_points: Merge keeps history and adds a merge commit
Rebase rewrites commits for a linear history
Never rebase shared, already-pushed history
red_flags: Force-pushing a rebased shared branch without coordination
Saying rebase and merge give an identical commit graph
follow_ups: How do you resolve a merge conflict?

question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING in SQL?
ideal_answer: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and aggregation, so it cannot use aggregate functions. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and can use aggregates such as COUNT or SUM. Filtering with WHERE first is usually more efficient because it reduces the rows to be grouped.
key_points: WHERE filters rows before GROUP BY
HAVING filters aggregated groups after GROUP BY
Prefer WHERE for row filters for performance
red_flags: Using aggregate functions inside WHERE
Moving row-level filters into HAVING unnecessarily
follow_ups: Write a query for departments with more than 5 employees.

question: Design a URL shortener like bit.ly. What are the main components and tradeoffs?
ideal_answer: Clarify requirements: create short links, redirect fast, high read-to-write ratio. Generate a unique short code, for example a base62 encoding of a counter or ID, store the mapping in a database, and serve redirects with a cache in front for hot links. Scale with a load balancer, database sharding or replication, and handle collisions, expiry, analytics, and abuse.
key_points: Requirements first: read-heavy, low-latency redirects
Short code via base62 of a unique ID; store code-to-URL mapping
Cache hot links; scale reads with replicas/sharding
red_flags: Jumping straight to technology without clarifying requirements
Using random codes with no collision handling
follow_ups: How would you generate unique IDs across multiple servers?

question: How do hash tables handle collisions, and how does the load factor affect performance?
ideal_answer: A collision happens when two keys map to the same bucket. Chaining stores colliding entries in a list per bucket, while open addressing probes for another free slot using linear probing, quadratic probing, or double hashing. As the load factor (entries divided by buckets) rises, collisions increase, so tables resize and rehash at a threshold to keep operations near O(1) on average.
key_points: Chaining vs open addressing (linear, quadratic, double hashing)
High load factor increases collisions and slows lookups
Resize and rehash to restore average O(1)
red_flags: Claiming hash tables never have collisions
Ignoring worst-case O(n) with a poor hash function
follow_ups: Why does resizing cost O(n) but stay amortized O(1)?
What makes a good hash function?
